summary: Describes the overall architecture for Deterministic Networking, which carries chosen unicast or multicast flows for real-time applications with very low loss and bounded latency inside a network domain. Techniques include reserving resources along the path, using explicit routes, and spreading packets over time or space for protection against path loss.

plainLanguage.summary: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) is designed for selected flows that need bounded delivery latency and very low packet loss. It reserves resources, can protect traffic across paths, and keeps routes stable within a controlled network domain.

subtitle: An architecture for bounded-latency, very-low-loss flows inside a controlled network domain.

tldr.problem: Real-time flows can fail when packet loss or worst-case delay exceeds application limits; average delay alone does not guarantee timely delivery.
tldr.mechanism: DetNet combines resource allocation, service protection across paths and explicit routes, using data-plane functions and a control architecture to provision flows.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the architecture for later DetNet data-plane work. It scopes DetNet to a single administrative domain or closed group, not the open Internet.

facts.label: Core techniques
facts.value: Resource allocation, service protection and explicit routes

today: RFC 8655 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2019. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the RFC describes an architecture for DetNet data-plane specifications.

sections.title: What Deterministic Networking Is For
sections.content:
DetNet provides delivery of specified unicast or multicast flows with extremely low packet loss and bounded end-to-end latency. It is intended for networks under one administrative control or a closed group of controls, such as a campus network or private WAN. The RFC says it is not intended for large groups of domains such as the Internet.

DetNet operates at the IP layer and can deliver service over lower-layer technologies such as MPLS and IEEE 802.1 Time-Sensitive Networking. It dedicates bandwidth and buffer space to flows and may replicate packets over multiple paths. Unused reserved resources can serve non-DetNet packets when the guarantees remain satisfied.
sections.plainLanguage: DetNet is for selected traffic that must arrive within defined latency limits and with very low loss. It is intended for a network domain with shared administrative control.

sections.title: The Quality of Service DetNet Targets
sections.content:
DetNet quality of service includes minimum and maximum end-to-end latency, bounded jitter, packet loss under stated node and link failure assumptions, and a limit on out-of-order delivery. Some applications cannot tolerate packet misordering.

The architecture focuses on worst-case latency, jitter and misordering rather than average values. A scheme that gives good average latency may still fail an application if its worst-case delay is too high. DetNet also aims to coexist with ordinary traffic and prevent misbehaving flows from consuming reserved resources.
sections.plainLanguage: DetNet focuses on the worst delay and loss a flow may experience, not just its average. Those limits matter to applications that cannot tolerate a late or missing packet.

sections.title: Three Techniques for DetNet Service
sections.content:
Resource allocation assigns buffer space and link bandwidth to a flow or aggregate along its path. The source must stay within a maximum packet size and transmission rate, and traffic must be limited and shaped at the network's ingress.

Service protection spreads data across paths to address random errors and equipment failures. Packet Replication, Elimination and Ordering Functions (PREOF) add or use sequencing information, copy packets to member flows, discard duplicates and restore order. Explicit routes keep a flow's path from changing immediately when network topology changes. The techniques may be used alone or together.
sections.plainLanguage: DetNet can reserve bandwidth and buffers, send copies over multiple paths, and keep a flow on an explicit route. A network can use one or combine several of these techniques.

sections.title: Service and Forwarding Sub-Layers
sections.content:
DetNet functionality is divided into adjacent service and forwarding sub-layers. The service sub-layer provides functions such as packet sequencing, replication, duplicate elimination, merging and packet encoding. The forwarding sub-layer supports the service with resource allocation and explicit routes.

Not every application or network needs every function, and the RFC says the separation is useful but not a formal requirement. Example service-sub-layer technologies include pseudowires, UDP and GRE; example forwarding-sub-layer technologies include IPv4, IPv6 and MPLS paths.
sections.plainLanguage: The service sub-layer handles protection and ordering of packets. The forwarding sub-layer reserves resources and provides routes; a deployment can use only the functions it needs.

sections.title: Nodes, Flows and Control Planes
sections.content:
DetNet has edge, relay and transit nodes. Edge nodes can connect end systems to the service sub-layer, relay nodes provide service functions across paths, and transit nodes forward traffic at the forwarding sub-layer. End systems may be unaware of DetNet or aware of its forwarding, service or both sub-layers.

The architecture separates the Application Plane, Controller Plane and Network Plane. Applications request service using a traffic specification; controller functions compute paths and install per-flow, per-hop behavior; network devices carry the packets. Synchronous flows use closely synchronized clocks, typically better than 1 microsecond, while asynchronous flows are described by packet size, observation interval and transmission count.
sections.plainLanguage: Applications describe the traffic they need, controller functions compute paths and set up network behavior, and devices forward the packets. Resources must be reserved before an application starts its DetNet flow.

sections.title: Scheduling, Flow Identification and Scale
sections.content:
Reserving resources alone does not establish bounded latency. Queuing, shaping and scheduling algorithms control when packets use buffers and links. The RFC lists credit-based shaping, time-gated queues, synchronized buffers and Ethernet frame preemption as examples.

At technology borders, a node may add a domain-specific Flow-ID so a lower layer can identify an individual flow without inspecting higher-layer packet fields. Flow identifiers must be unique within their domain. Aggregating flows can reduce the amount of per-flow state needed in each node.
sections.plainLanguage: Scheduling rules control when packets use reserved resources. When traffic crosses between technologies, a node can add a flow identifier that the next technology understands.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
DetNet inherits security properties from the IP, MPLS or other technologies it uses. Security work includes controlling who can request resources, protecting data confidentiality, and maintaining the availability of the promised service. The RFC highlights accurate, available and trustworthy time synchronization as critical.

Per-flow identification can reveal information about traffic and let an observer correlate flows or select them for inspection. Admission control and filtering can help limit traffic from malicious or malfunctioning devices.
sections.plainLanguage: DetNet needs controls on who can reserve resources and on traffic entering the domain. Flow labels and time synchronization also have security and privacy consequences.
